title: A deep energy method formulation for phase-field modelling of ductile fracture
authors: Nojus Plungė, Peter Brommer, Rachel S. Edwards, Emmanouil G. Kakouris
abstract: This work extends the Deep Energy Method to phase-field modelling of ductile fracture in elasto-plastic solids. Its key contribution is an incremental DEM-based formulation that couples history-dependent J2 plasticity and plasticity-dependent fracture toughness with separate energy-optimised displacement and phase-field representations. The formulation combines the second-order Ambrosio-Tortorelli phase-field fracture model with small-strain J2 plasticity and linear isotropic hardening. A volumetric-deviatoric split defines the elastic crack-driving energy, while accumulated equivalent plastic strain governs the degradation of local fracture toughness. Plastic internal variables are updated locally through radial return. The reduced energy is minimised alternately with respect to the displacement and phase fields, represented by a ReZero residual neural network and spatially localised Gaussian radial basis functions with trainable centres, respectively. This split addresses the diffuse phase-field profiles observed in preliminary calculations with a shared global network. Alternating optimisation is combined with transfer learning to reuse trainable parameters and optimiser states across loading increments, while the converged constitutive history is carried forward separately at quadrature points. The numerical results demonstrate close agreement with finite-element reference solutions in predicting force-displacement responses, energy evolution, plastic deformation and crack propagation. The framework captures the main features of ductile fracture, although accuracy becomes more sensitive to loading increments near abrupt fracture events.

infographic.key_insight: An incremental Deep Energy Method can model ductile fracture by coupling J2 plasticity and phase-field fracture with separate neural representations for displacement and crack phase.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a physics-informed, mesh-free alternative for predicting elastic-plastic damage and crack growth in ductile solids with good agreement to finite-element references.
method: Uses small-strain J2 plasticity with linear isotropic hardening and a second-order Ambrosio-Tortorelli phase-field fracture model.
Represents displacement with a ReZero residual neural network and the phase field with localized Gaussian radial basis functions.
Minimizes reduced energy alternately across loading increments, with radial return updates and transfer learning for history variables.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports close agreement with finite-element solutions for force-displacement response, energy evolution, plastic deformation, and crack propagation.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy becomes more sensitive to the loading increment size near abrupt fracture events, so incremental step control is important.
infographic.paper_title: A deep energy method formulation for phase-field modelling of ductile fracture

title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models
authors: Shuoran Jiang, Wentao Zhu, Yang Xiang, Dongfeng Li, Yunan Zhang, Mengchen Zhao
abstract: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that large language models contain functionally specialized subnetworks with very low overlap, and that isolating updates to these regions can improve continual learning while reducing catastrophic forgetting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For AI systems that must adapt over time, localized parameter updates offer a more efficient and stable alternative to full-model retraining, preserving prior capabilities under sequential learning.
method: Use gradient-attribution profiling to identify cognition-associated functional subnetworks.
Route each training example to its corresponding subnetwork for targeted adaptation.
Restrict parameter updates and optimizer states to the selected regions in CiMEO.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was evaluated on 1.4 million sequential instructions and achieved the best average performance across five generative benchmarks covering programming, exam-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning.
infographic.watch_item: Subnetwork localization and routing add implementation complexity, and the approach depends on accurately identifying task-relevant regions without missing shared representations.
infographic.paper_title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models

title: Time to Fake It: Continual Machine Learning Intensifies Unfairness in Deepfake Detection
authors: Kajaree Das, Oliver Böse, Subarnaduti Paul, Gabriel Storch, Martin Mundt
abstract: Deepfake detectors safeguard against misinformation, rendering their failures as much a societal as a technical concern. As generators constantly evolve, detectors trained on static datasets miss newly arising threats, while progressive training interferes catastrophically. Yet, mitigating forgetfulness in terms of accuracy, the prevalent focus of continual learning (CL), is insufficient to reflect real-world impact. We therefore scrutinize the effects of CL methods with respect to evolving fairness. To this end, we analyze four dimensions of fairness across diverse demographics for detectors trained progressively on a chronological sequence of 11 real-world deepfake generation methods. Tracking fairness metrics over time, we expose non-trivial interplays between performance and fairness that depend on both the choice of CL algorithm and demographic intersections. We find accuracy degradation to typically exacerbate unfairness and, conversely, fairness improvements to remain scarce over time. Dissecting the CL method families (rehearsal, prompts, regularization), we observe that inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone, but likely entangled with representation learning. We thus issue a call to action for CL methods to take social outcomes into account when balancing the stability-plasticity tradeoff.

infographic.key_insight: Continual learning for deepfake detectors can worsen demographic unfairness over time, so preserving accuracy alone is not enough.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For real-world security systems, model updates must be evaluated not just for robustness to new attacks but also for shifting fairness across demographic groups.
method: Evaluated continual-learning deepfake detectors on a chronological sequence of 11 real-world generation methods.
Tracked four fairness dimensions across diverse demographics and demographic intersections over time.
Compared CL families including rehearsal, prompts, and regularization to study performance–fairness tradeoffs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study analyzes fairness metrics over time on 11 sequential deepfake generation methods, showing that accuracy drops often coincide with increased unfairness.
infographic.watch_item: Fairness gains were scarce and inequitable forgetting was not fully explained by underrepresentation, so mitigation may require changes to representation learning rather than only data balancing.
infographic.paper_title: Time to Fake It: Continual Machine Learning Intensifies Unfairness in Deepfake Detection

title: Modeling Transport and Mechanics in Anion Exchange Membranes to Optimize Continuous CO2 Separations
authors: Samaneh Bayati, Jennifer Wade, Sara Sarbaz, Heidi Feigenbaum, Horacio Lopez-Marques, Winston Wang
abstract: Water transport in charged polymer membranes is strongly influenced by hydration-dependent transport properties and polymer-network deformation. Under water-activity gradients, spatial variations in water concentration induce swelling and mechanical stresses, while the resulting deformation can influence water transport. Capturing this bidirectional interaction is important for predicting membrane behavior under nonuniform hydration conditions. This study develops a transient finite element model of water transport and mechanical deformation in a Fumasep FAA-3-50 anion exchange membrane. The framework incorporates concentration-dependent water diffusivity, hygroscopic swelling, and nonlinear viscoelastic polymer response. Uncoupled, one-way coupled, and fully coupled formulations are compared to distinguish the effects of hydration-dependent diffusivity and mechanical coupling. In the fully coupled model, local water concentration governs swelling and mechanical response, while deformation, evolving membrane geometry, and mechanical pressure feed back into water transport. Simulations predict spatially and temporally nonuniform swelling and deformation that track the evolving water-concentration field. Relative to the uncoupled concentration-dependent diffusion model, mechanical feedback alters the predicted transport response, although transport remains primarily diffusion-driven. The fully coupled model is validated against steady-state water-transport measurements across water-activity gradients and reproduces the experimentally observed hydration dependence, with strongest agreement at intermediate hydration levels. These results highlight the importance of coupled hydration, swelling, deformation, and transport processes in models of hydrated anion exchange membranes and provide a framework for evaluating membrane behavior in moisture-facilitated transport applications.

infographic.key_insight: Water transport in anion exchange membranes is bidirectionally coupled to swelling and mechanics, so hydration-dependent deformation changes the predicted diffusion response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate CO2-separation membrane design needs models that capture both concentration-dependent transport and mechanical feedback under nonuniform hydration.
method: Transient finite element model for water transport + deformation in Fumasep FAA-3-50 AEM
Includes concentration-dependent diffusivity, hygroscopic swelling, and nonlinear viscoelastic response
Compares uncoupled, one-way coupled, and fully coupled formulations
infographic.evidence_signal: The fully coupled model was validated against steady-state water-transport measurements across water-activity gradients and matched the observed hydration dependence best at intermediate hydration.
infographic.watch_item: The model is still primarily diffusion-driven, so mechanical coupling may be less critical in regimes where hydration gradients and deformation are weak.
infographic.paper_title: Modeling Transport and Mechanics in Anion Exchange Membranes to Optimize Continuous CO2 Separations

title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models
authors: Jie Li, Youming Tao, Bowei He, Meng Ding
abstract: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all three base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.

infographic.key_insight: Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU) shows that robust unlearning should block relearning of removed knowledge without harming a model’s ability to learn new tasks after later fine-tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For deployed LLMs that keep getting updated, UMU offers a practical way to preserve safety and privacy while maintaining post-update adaptability.
method: Apply the same simulated relearning update to both the defended model and an undefended reference starting from the same unlearned checkpoint.
Use an update-matched reference instead of a pre-update reference when judging whether the model should stay close after an update.
Select the defended model using new-task learning performance to balance suppression and plasticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: On TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models, UMU improved relearning resistance and plasticity across three base unlearning methods, reducing harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while increasing new-task accuracy by 3.5 points.
infographic.watch_item: If the reference is not updated consistently, evaluation can falsely reward over-conservative models that resist relearning but also lose plasticity.
infographic.paper_title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models

title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions
authors: Kidus Abebe, David Gaetano, Aurelia Moriyama-Gurish, Jana Šmilauerová, Yanfei Gao, Udo D. Schwarz
abstract: Ti-15Mo (wt%) is a well-established $β$-stabilized alloy whose mechanical response is strongly governed by phase stability and deformation mechanisms that operate at the single-grain scale. Because these intragranular mechanisms are intrinsically anisotropic, understanding the orientation dependence of the elastic and plastic response is critical to the texture-engineered processing of wrought components. Here, we quantify the nanomechanical anisotropy of single-crystal Ti-15Mo by combining EBSD with nanoindentation to correlate hardness, indentation modulus, strain rate sensitivity, and indentation yield response with the crystallographic surface normal near $\langle111\rangle,\langle124\rangle,\langle011\rangle,\langle023\rangle$, and $\langle013\rangle$ directions. While the modulus anisotropy is small (~10%), contrary to the prediction for a cubic crystal with A>1, orientations near $\langle111\rangle$ exhibit the lowest moduli. Yield onset is likewise softest near $\langle111\rangle$ and spans 41%, while hardness spans only 6.6% and follows neither the modulus nor the yield ordering. The alloy also exhibits yield behavior not captured by the simple CRSS/Schmid-factor models evaluated here. Strain-rate-jump tests yield V*=18-31b$^3$, consistent with kink-pair-nucleation-controlled plasticity; based on V*, the orientations separate into two groups suggestive of glide-dominated versus twin/transformation-participating response. We reveal an inversion of the elastic anisotropy expected for a homogeneous cubic $β$-phase and an orientation-dependent yield-onset response that is not reproduced by the simple Schmid-factor models examined here. Retained athermal $ω$ is proposed as the contributor because $β\rightarrowω$ collapse occurs on {111}$_β$ planes and may provide anelastic compliance through the reversible $ω\rightarrowβ$ transformation.

infographic.key_insight: Single-crystal Ti-15Mo shows orientation-dependent nanoindentation behavior that reverses the expected cubic elastic anisotropy and produces yield-onset trends that simple Schmid-factor/CRSS models cannot explain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For texture engineering and component design, the study shows that local grain orientation can strongly alter elastic compliance and yielding, so single-phase cubic assumptions may miss critical anisotropy in β-Ti alloys.
method: EBSD to identify crystallographic surface normals of indented single crystals
Nanoindentation mapping of hardness, indentation modulus, and yield onset across multiple orientations
Strain-rate-jump testing to estimate activation volume and infer deformation mechanism
infographic.evidence_signal: Across orientations near <111>, <124>, <011>, <023>, and <013>, the authors report ~10% modulus anisotropy, 41% yield-onset spread, only 6.6% hardness variation, and activation volumes of 18–31 b^3.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism assignment is still inferential: the proposed role of retained athermal ω and the rejection of simple Schmid/CRSS predictions need confirmation with direct phase- and slip-system-resolved measurements.
infographic.paper_title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions

title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration
authors: Wenpu Du, Peng Zhou, Yunlong Xia, Sinuo Xin, Congcong Zhang, Boyang Zhang
abstract: The penetration-resistant design of concrete structures requires the spatiotemporal evolution of the stress field within the target, whereas in design only the strength grade, the geometry and the projectile parameters are known, and the aggregate arrangement is not. Empirical formulae and scalar-output surrogates serve design screening, and mesoscale finite element models resolve the aggregate-scale response, but one solution cannot cover random aggregate samples at scale, and no framework links mesoscale heterogeneity to field-level prediction. A physics-coupled graph neural operator (PC-GNO) is proposed, which learns in function space the evolution of the mid-plane six-component stress tensor field. The training data are generated by full-scale, aggregate-resolved finite element models and comprise 359 cases at the impact velocities of 100, 135 and 165 m/s, corresponding to compressive strengths of 14, 23 and 48 MPa; the data source is verified by laboratory measurements. The coupling strength of message passing is constructed from the impedance contrast across the material interface, and the update is constrained by spectral normalization. Under the single-step primary setting, the mean accuracy of the three levels is 80.16% (91.45%, 77.80% and 71.22%), i.e. 27.81, 42.46 and 34.16 percentage points above the preceding-frame field of the same window; with 20 664 parameters it exceeds the 87.9% of the best Fourier neural operator configuration (about 812 times as many parameters) and the 71.0% of the closed-form linear regression. The output is the complete six-component tensor field rather than a fixed engineering quantity, so that strength criteria and energy indicators follow from one set of weights. For field-level response prediction in concrete penetration, this result provides a data-driven route, with conditions of applicability defined by the training and the evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: PC-GNO learns the full mid-plane six-component stress tensor field in concrete penetration by coupling graph neural operator updates with physics-informed interface impedance and spectral normalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables field-level surrogate prediction for penetration-resistant concrete design, linking mesoscale aggregate heterogeneity to actionable stress and energy-response maps.
method: Train on aggregate-resolved FEM penetration simulations in function space
Use impedance contrast across material interfaces to set message-passing strength
Constrain updates with spectral normalization to stabilize field evolution
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 359 validated FEM cases at 100, 135, and 165 m/s for concrete strengths of 14, 23, and 48 MPa, PC-GNO reached 80.16% mean accuracy and outperformed both a strong Fourier neural operator baseline and linear regression.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability is limited to the velocity, strength, and geometry regimes represented in the training/evaluation data, so extrapolation beyond those conditions should be treated cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration

title: Co2In: a Bi-level Memory Incremental Learning Framework with Knowledge Encoding, Consolidation, and Integration
authors: Wenju Sun, Qingyong Li, Boyang Li, Wen Wang, Siyu Zhang, Yi Wei
abstract: Incremental learning (IL) aims to continually acquire new knowledge (plasticity) while retaining previously learned information (stability). However, striking a balance between plasticity and stability remains a significant challenge for intelligent systems. The human brain achieves exceptional balance, owing to various memory units that collaboratively encode and store information. Inspired by human memory mechanisms, this paper introduces an IL framework with knowledge enCoding, Consolidation, and Integration (Co2In). Co2In is designed as a bi-level memory architecture: a working memory for adaptive knowledge acquisition and a long-term memory dedicated to the persistent retention of information. The two memory modules work cooperatively during IL. The working memory first learns from new data to encode knowledge into parameters. Subsequently, Co2In performs a consolidation process to identify underlying patterns in the learned parameters and re-express them into a compact knowledge representation. Next, the knowledge representation and the identified patterns are transformed into separate network layers and integrated into the long-term memory. These designs empower Co2In to accumulate knowledge with high plasticity and stability. We evaluate Co2In on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL settings. Experimental results show that Co2In achieves state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory consumption.

infographic.key_insight: Co2In improves continual learning by separating fast adaptive learning in working memory from durable retention in long-term memory, then consolidating and integrating learned knowledge into compact representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For data-driven constitutive modeling, this suggests a practical route to update material models with new experiments while reducing catastrophic forgetting of previously learned behaviors.
method: Working memory learns new-task parameters from incoming data to preserve plasticity.
Consolidation extracts patterns from learned parameters into compact knowledge representations.
Integrated long-term memory stores transformed knowledge in separate network layers for stable retention.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework was evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet in exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL settings, where it achieved state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory use.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of consolidation and integration; in real deployments, added architectural complexity may increase implementation and tuning burden.
infographic.paper_title: Co2In: a Bi-level Memory Incremental Learning Framework with Knowledge Encoding, Consolidation, and Integration

title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays
authors: Gang Liu, Chen Yang, Junyan Hu, Jianguo Chen, Lixin Duan
abstract: Systolic arrays are widely used to accelerate neural-network inference, yet fixed two-dimensional arrays struggle with the substantial diversity in both matrix geometry and available parallelism across CNNs and Transformer-based large language models. This mismatch is particularly severe for skinny matrices, small-batch autoregressive decoding, and operators containing multiple independent partitions, leading to low processing-element (PE) utilization and repeated spatial folding. Existing reconfigurable arrays typically improve either shape adaptation or distributed execution, whereas supporting both through fine-grained routing incurs considerable interconnect, buffering, and control overheads. We present LizTail (named after lizard tail autotomy, where predefined fracture planes allow segments to detach and remain independently active, analogous to LizTail's predefined reconfiguration boundaries), a multi-mode systolic array that enables constrained segment-level reconfiguration by partitioning a $128\times128$ array into 32 regular $128\times4$ segments and adding connectivity only at predefined endpoints. The resulting substrate supports trimming, long-path extension through $180^\circ$ turn-back connections, and distributed execution in which each subarray can itself be trimmed or extended. Differentiated PE datapaths and segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers provide the required compute and data-delivery flexibility without unrestricted PE-level routing. A hardware-constrained mapper selects the execution organization, dataflow, task partition, and tiling. Across representative workloads, LizTail achieves geometric-mean speedups of $5.02\times$ on CNN inference and $25.67\times$ on LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, while reducing EDP by up to $38.23\times$. LizTail is open-sourced at https://github.com/kmjbwxa/LizTail.

infographic.key_insight: LizTail unifies shape adaptation and spatial parallelism by splitting a 128×128 systolic array into reconfigurable 128×4 segments, letting the hardware both fit awkward matrix shapes and execute independent sub-tasks efficiently.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for AI accelerators because CNNs and especially autoregressive LLM decoding often leave fixed arrays underutilized, so segment-level reconfiguration can raise PE utilization without the cost of full PE-level routing.
method: Partitions the array into 32 regular segments with connectivity only at predefined endpoints.
Supports trimming, 180° turn-back extension, and distributed execution across subarrays.
Uses differentiated PE datapaths plus segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers, with a hardware-constrained mapper choosing execution mode and tiling.
infographic.evidence_signal: On representative workloads, the design reports geometric-mean speedups of 5.02× for CNN inference and 25.67× for LLM decoding versus a TPU-like array, with EDP reductions up to 38.23×.
infographic.watch_item: The added flexibility still depends on constrained predefined boundaries and custom mapping, so real performance may be sensitive to compiler quality, workload fit, and hardware implementation overheads.
infographic.paper_title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays

title: Low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations
authors: Joy Saha, Jun Yang, Peimeng Yin
abstract: In this work, we develop low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations and incorporate them into a basis-update \& Galerkin mass-lumped finite element method (\mbox{BUG-MLFEM}). By incorporating mass lumping via Gauss-Lobatto quadrature, the spatial discretization yields a matrix differential equation equipped with diagonal positive-definite mass matrices. We establish the weighted dynamical low-rank approximation (WDLRA) within the Galerkin framework of the MLFEM system, proving the theoretical equivalence between the BUG integrator and MLFEM on low-rank subspaces, which guarantees the discrete well-posedness of the implicit BUG steps. To overcome the severe computational bottleneck of standard $O(m^3+n^3)$ Sylvester solvers, we develop tailored, low-cost non-iterative solvers that exploit the inherent sparse-by-small algebraic structure. Under Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions (BCs), the large coefficient matrices are banded, enabling efficient diagonalization of the small $r \times r$ factor matrix and reducing the per-step computational complexity to $O((m+n)r^2)$ and storage to $O((m+n)r)$. For periodic BCs, we combine this diagonalization strategy with a rank-2 Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update to handle wrap-around corner entries at negligible additional cost. Numerical experiments demonstrate first-order temporal and $(k+1)$th-order spatial convergence of the proposed BUG-MLFEM in the discrete $L^2$ norm, where $k$ denotes the polynomial degree of the finite element space, together with significant computational speedups over existing low-rank integrators.

infographic.key_insight: The paper couples mass-lumped finite elements with weighted dynamical low-rank approximation and fast non-iterative Sylvester solvers to make reaction-diffusion simulation cheaper without sacrificing accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, lower-memory time stepping for large PDE discretizations, which is useful for scalable multiphysics and reduced-order simulation workflows.
method: Use BUG-MLFEM with Gauss-Lobatto mass lumping to obtain diagonal positive-definite mass matrices.
Formulate weighted dynamical low-rank approximation on the Galerkin MLFEM system and prove equivalence on low-rank subspaces.
Replace costly iterative Sylvester solves with structure-exploiting non-iterative solvers; for periodic BCs, add a rank-2 Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports first-order temporal and (k+1)-th-order spatial convergence in discrete L2 norm, plus substantial speedups over existing low-rank integrators.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on structured sparse/banded matrices and careful handling of boundary conditions, so implementation complexity may rise for more general meshes or operators.
infographic.paper_title: Low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations

title: Neural Spline Flow Diffeomorphisms for Pullback Finite Element Methods on Complex Domains
authors: Ioannis Kalogeris, Anaksagoras Spitas, Konstantinos Atzarakis, George Stavroulakis, Vissarion Papadopoulos
abstract: We propose a method for solving partial differential equations on complex domains by learning smooth, invertible mappings from a fixed reference domain using Neural Spline Flows (NSFs). Monotone rational-quadratic spline coupling layers ensure a strictly positive Jacobian determinant by construction, eliminating the need for Jacobian-sign penalties. A diffeomorphic pullback transfers the weak form of the PDE to the reference domain, enabling finite element analysis on reusable structured meshes. To generalize across shapes, a shared NSF is conditioned on low-dimensional latent codes learned through an auto-decoder framework; a subsequent encoder predicts these codes for unseen geometries in a single forward pass. For a given learned map, the pullback preserves the mathematical structure of the PDE and is exactly equivalent to solving on the domain represented by that map. Because the learned domain generally approximates the target geometry, geometric mapping error remains distinct from finite element discretization and quadrature errors. Numerical benchmarks show that sufficiently accurate learned mappings yield reliable finite element solutions. By avoiding repeated generation of unstructured meshes, the method addresses a bottleneck in simulation workflows. The fixed reference mesh also creates opportunities for efficient assembly, memory-aligned data access, and precomputed quadrature. The resulting framework assigns geometric complexity to the neural network while retaining conventional finite element discretization and convergence properties on the learned domain, with overall accuracy also governed by geometric fidelity.

infographic.key_insight: The paper learns smooth, invertible Neural Spline Flow mappings from a fixed reference mesh to complex geometries, so finite element PDEs can be solved on reusable structured meshes via a diffeomorphic pullback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can reduce the need for repeated unstructured mesh generation while preserving standard FEM structure, making simulation workflows faster and more reusable for complex-shaped domains.
method: Use monotone rational-quadratic spline coupling layers to guarantee a positive Jacobian determinant and diffeomorphic mapping.
Transfer the PDE weak form to a reference domain with a pullback FEM formulation on a fixed structured mesh.
Condition a shared NSF on low-dimensional latent geometry codes, with an encoder for one-shot prediction on unseen shapes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical benchmarks showing that when the learned mapping is sufficiently accurate, the resulting finite element solutions are reliable and the method remains equivalent to solving on the represented domain.
infographic.watch_item: Overall solution accuracy still depends on geometric fidelity, so mapping error can become the dominant source of error if the learned geometry is not accurate enough.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Spline Flow Diffeomorphisms for Pullback Finite Element Methods on Complex Domains

title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers
authors: Zhouhan Zhong, Qiuhong Shen, Xingyi Yang, Jinyi Xu, Xinchao Wang
abstract: 3D part assembly aims to reconstruct a complete shape from a set of unassembled parts by predicting a rigid SE(3) transformation for each part. Because the placement of a part is rarely determined by its own geometry, the task demands reasoning over the entire part set, and existing methods, which rely on pairwise relations or iterative generation and verification, scale poorly to objects with many parts. We present LLM2R, which casts part assembly as sequence modeling with a pretrained decoder-only large language model (LLM): a Point-BERT encoder and a Q-Former compress each part into a block of geometric tokens, the blocks of all parts are concatenated, and a causal LLM adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) processes the sequence in one forward pass. Causal attention, however, lets the hidden states of a part observe only the parts that precede it. LLM2R therefore appends a block of learnable summary tokens after the last part: these tokens follow every part, so their states aggregate the whole assembly at a constant token cost, and a part-aware pose head fuses each part's states with them before predicting its rotation and translation. One architecture thus handles semantic and geometric assembly and predicts all poses in a single non-autoregressive pass. LLM2R achieves the highest part accuracy and success rate on all three PartNet categories, the best rotation error, translation error, and part accuracy on PartNeXt, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on Breaking Bad, where only a fracture-specialized method is more accurate. Its advantage grows with the number of parts: at 100 parts it exceeds GARF by 33.5 points in part accuracy on Breaking Bad and Assembler by 29.1 points on PartNet, and it transfers zero-shot to unseen categories with more than 16 points higher part accuracy than the strongest of three baselines.

infographic.key_insight: LLM2R turns 3D part assembly into a single-pass sequence modeling problem, using a pretrained decoder-only LLM with summary tokens to reason over all parts and predict every rigid pose at once.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster and more scalable reconstruction of fractured or disassembled 3D objects, especially when assemblies contain many parts and pairwise methods become inefficient.
method: Encode each part with Point-BERT + Q-Former into geometric token blocks.
Concatenate all part blocks and process them with a LoRA-adapted causal LLM in one forward pass.
Append learnable summary tokens so each part's pose head can fuse local and global context before predicting SE(3) transform.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method reports top performance across PartNet, PartNeXt, and Breaking Bad, with especially large gains as part count increases and strong zero-shot transfer to unseen categories.
infographic.watch_item: Because causal attention is directional, the model depends on the ordering of part blocks, so sequence design and token budget may affect robustness and reproducibility.
infographic.paper_title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers

title: FEM-Validated Real-Time Modelling of Soft Tactile Deformation
authors: Silvia Terrile, Kaichen Shi, Taejun Kwon, Jiseok Lee, Nathan Lepora, Yeejin Lee
abstract: Accurate modelling of soft tactile sensors remains difficult because finite element methods (FEM) are computa- tionally expensive, while real-time simulators often lack fidelity for hyperelastic deformation. Large physical datasets are also impractical to collect because repeated testing can damage fragile sensors. We present a data-efficient framework that combines limited real-world validation, high-fidelity FEM, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for accurate real-time prediction of two-dimensional tactile deformation in a planar soft tactile structure. The key idea is to decouple validation from training: 82 camera-tracked contact configurations are used only to tune and validate an ANSYS FEM model, which then generates 768 synthetic contact scenarios for GNN training. We evaluate both forward prediction from marker deformation to contact localisation and inverse inference from contact configuration to marker deformation. The validated FEM achieves sub-0.5 mm error in more than 90% of validation cases, while the learned GNN surrogate reaches a mean absolute error of 0.32 mm with millisecond-scale inference, compared with minute-scale FEM simulation. Models trained entirely on synthetic FEM data retain sub-millimetre accuracy on real measurements from the 2D tactile structure, demonstrating strong sim-to-real transfer within the tested planar setting. We further integrate the learned model into a real-time visualisation pipeline, enabling rapid deformation prediction for virtual prototyping and simulator-based design exploration without extensive physical testing.

infographic.key_insight: A FEM-validated graph neural network can deliver real-time, sub-millimetre prediction of soft tactile deformation using only a small set of physical validations plus synthetic FEM data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables fast, accurate virtual prototyping of planar soft tactile sensors and contact localization without expensive repeated physical testing or minute-scale simulation.
method: Use 82 camera-tracked real contact cases to tune and validate an ANSYS FEM model.
Generate 768 synthetic contact scenarios from the validated FEM for GNN training.
Deploy the trained GNN for forward and inverse deformation prediction in a real-time visualization pipeline.
infographic.evidence_signal: The validated FEM achieved under 0.5 mm error in over 90% of validation cases, and the GNN reached 0.32 mm mean absolute error with millisecond-scale inference on the 2D tactile structure.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated sim-to-real transfer is strongest for the tested planar setting, so performance may not directly generalize to more complex geometries or loading conditions without revalidation.
infographic.paper_title: FEM-Validated Real-Time Modelling of Soft Tactile Deformation

title: Deep Learning-based Mechanical Characterization of Synthetically Generated Plant Fibers under Transverse Compression
authors: Nikolaos Kegkeroglou, Bilal Sabillah, Myrto Inglezou, Vincent Placet, Céndric Clevy, Antonios Porichis
abstract: Plant fibers are increasingly used as sustainable reinforcements in composites, but the intrinsic variability of their microstructure causes substantial scatter in transverse mechanical behavior, complicating composite design. Characterizing this behavior relies on finite element (FE) simulations requiring several minutes of high-performance computing per fiber, making high-throughput characterization across realistic fiber populations impractical. In this study, we propose a deep learning framework replacing this FE bottleneck with a fast pipeline. It includes two coupled recursive U-Nets predicting the step-by-step evolution of fiber deformation and internal stress fields under transverse compression, followed by a regression CNN estimating the transverse Young's modulus from the final stress field. Unlike prior approaches predicting stress fields for fixed configurations or idealized geometries, our framework recursively resolves the full temporal stress evolution for synthetic fibers derived from real hemp cross-sections, with or without a lumen. Trained on 1,000 synthetic fiber geometries with FE ground truth, it reproduces the stress field sequence with a Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) of $0.9574 \pm 0.0074$ and a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of $0.0345 \pm 0.0079$. It estimates transverse Young's modulus with an $R^2$ of $0.938 \pm 0.024$, a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of $24.31 \pm 1.23$ MPa, and a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of $5.25 \pm 0.91\%$. Inference requires under one second per fiber versus five minutes per FE simulation, drastically reducing computational cost. This offers a fast, reliable tool for mechanical characterization of synthetic plant fibers, with promising applications in designing natural fiber-reinforced composites.

infographic.key_insight: A recursive deep learning pipeline can replace slow finite-element simulation to predict the full transverse compression response of synthetic plant fibers and their effective modulus.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables fast, scalable screening of plant-fiber microstructures for composite design, reducing per-fiber analysis from minutes to under one second.
method: Two coupled recursive U-Nets predict stepwise deformation and internal stress evolution under transverse compression.
A regression CNN estimates transverse Young's modulus from the final stress field.
Trained on 1,000 synthetic hemp-derived fiber geometries with FE ground truth, including cases with and without a lumen.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model achieved SSIM 0.9574 ± 0.0074 and RMSE 0.0345 ± 0.0079 for stress-field evolution, and predicted Young's modulus with R^2 = 0.938 ± 0.024, MAE = 24.31 ± 1.23 MPa, and MAPE = 5.25 ± 0.91%.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on synthetic geometries trained against FE data, so generalization to experimental fibers with unresolved microstructural defects or manufacturing variability still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Learning-based Mechanical Characterization of Synthetically Generated Plant Fibers under Transverse Compression

title: An algebraic multiscale framework for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners
authors: Filipe Cumaru, Hadi Hajibeygi, Cornelis Vuik, Alexander Heinlein
abstract: The robustness of two-level overlapping additive Schwarz (OAS) preconditioners for highly heterogeneous elliptic problems hinges on the choice of the coarse space. We propose an algebraic multiscale (AM) coarse space built from the system matrix alone through an algebraic formulation of the multiscale finite element method (MsFEM). The coarse basis functions are energy-minimizing extensions of the solutions of reduced boundary condition (RBC) problems on the subdomain interface, so that coefficient variations along the interface enter the coarse space. By posing the RBC problems on slabs that extend the interface, the construction also applies to general unstructured domain decompositions. Embedding the AM formulation in an energy-minimizing framework extends it to linear elasticity, and we show that existing condition number bounds for OAS with MsFEM coarse spaces carry over to the algebraic setting. For problems with high coefficient inclusions on the coarse nodes, the AM iteration count and condition number are unaffected by increasing the contrast. In 3D scalar diffusion with log-normal coefficients, AM needs about as many iterations as the generalized Dryja--Smith--Widlund (GDSW) coarse space, while solving a coarse problem ten times smaller. For linear elasticity, omitting the coarse basis functions associated with the rotational rigid body modes yields a fully algebraic coarse space that still scales well for homogeneous problems.

infographic.key_insight: The paper builds a fully algebraic multiscale coarse space for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners that preserves robustness for highly heterogeneous elliptic and elasticity problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a matrix-only route to scalable domain decomposition preconditioners, reducing coarse problem size while maintaining strong performance on difficult multiscale mechanics and diffusion cases.
method: Constructs coarse basis functions by solving algebraic reduced boundary condition (RBC) problems on subdomain interfaces.
Uses energy-minimizing extensions of interface solutions so coefficient variation is encoded in the coarse space.
Extends the framework to unstructured decompositions and linear elasticity via an energy-minimizing formulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports contrast-independent iteration counts for high-coefficient inclusions, and in 3D log-normal diffusion the method matches GDSW iteration counts while solving a coarse problem about 10× smaller.
infographic.watch_item: The fully algebraic elasticity variant drops rotational rigid-body basis functions, so robustness may depend on problem class and decomposition details.
infographic.paper_title: An algebraic multiscale framework for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners

title: Wavelength-selective bidirectional plasticity in self-powered Se/ZnMgO visual synapses
authors: Zacharie Jehl Li-Kao, Miho Akasaka, Myeongok Kim, Kunal J. Tiwari, Antoine Moore, Mykhailo A. Koltsov
abstract: Artificial visual synapses combine sensing, memory and processing in a single device, but most of them need an external voltage to read the synaptic weight and light is generally able to strengthen the weight rather than to weaken it. We report here Se/ZnMgO thin film photodiodes in which the photocurrent at zero bias writes and reads the synaptic weight, with a direction of change set by the photon energy alone. At equal photon flux, 365 nm pulses increase the photocurrent by 38 % while 455 nm pulses decrease it, and the depression reaching 30 % at higher flux, with up to 19 distinguishable levels per branch and no electrical energy spent. Spectrally resolved light soaking shows that short wavelengths potentiate while low-energy light erases. The interesting property is therefore the photon energy-dependent competition between potentiation and depression, the crossover being set by the defect population of the interface. Optical simulations show that both wavelengths are absorbed within the first tens of nanometres of Se, and the stored state is erased by a reverse bias in a voltage-dependent way and by sub-gap light, which indicates that potentiation corresponds to interface defects filled with electrons, in agreement with drift-diffusion simulations. The devices also show relearning, their response is modulated by bending on flexible substrates, and a network built from the measured weight updates reaches 89 % accuracy on handwritten digit recognition without noise and 85 % with the measured noise, against 97.5 % for floating-point weights.

infographic.key_insight: Se/ZnMgO photodiodes act as self-powered visual synapses whose weight can be potentiated or depressed purely by light wavelength, enabling zero-bias learning and readout.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a low-energy route to neuromorphic vision hardware that integrates sensing, memory, and computation in one flexible optoelectronic device.
method: Built Se/ZnMgO thin-film photodiodes operated at zero bias as artificial synapses
Used wavelength-selective optical pulses and light soaking to map potentiation/depression behavior
Interpreted the mechanism with optical simulations and drift-diffusion modeling of interfacial defect states
infographic.evidence_signal: At equal photon flux, 365 nm light increased photocurrent by 38% while 455 nm light decreased it, with up to 19 distinguishable levels per branch and digit-recognition accuracy of 89% ideal / 85% with measured noise.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on interfacial defect populations and optical conditions, so reproducibility and long-term stability may be sensitive to fabrication variability and device aging.
infographic.paper_title: Wavelength-selective bidirectional plasticity in self-powered Se/ZnMgO visual synapses

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D
authors: Tommaso Bevilacqua, Axel Klawonn, Martin Lanser, Adam Wasiak
abstract: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW) and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces for high-order finite element methods (FEM) and virtual element methods (VEM) are investigated and applied to the Poisson problem in 2D. The GDSW coarse space is a well-established robust choice for preconditioners in domain decomposition, while the RGDSW coarse space offers a competitive alternative by reducing the coarse problem dimension while maintaining robustness. On the theoretical side, a condition number bound for both preconditioners is proved for conforming $\mathbb{P}_k$ and $\mathbb{Q}_k$ finite element spaces with explicit dependence on the polynomial degree $k$. Through numerical experiments on structured triangular and quadrilateral meshes for FEM and on polygonal meshes for VEM, it is demonstrated that both GDSW and RGDSW maintain scalability properties across polynomial orders up to $k=9$ for selected degrees. The RGDSW approach achieves a reduction in the coarse problem dimension by a factor of approximately three compared to GDSW while maintaining competitive iteration counts.

infographic.key_insight: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW and RGDSW coarse spaces remain scalable for high-order 2D FEM/VEM Poisson problems, with RGDSW cutting coarse-space size substantially while preserving robustness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical preconditioning strategy for high-order finite element and virtual element solvers where iteration stability and coarse-solver cost strongly affect performance.
method: Develop two-level overlapping additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW and reduced GDSW coarse spaces.
Analyze condition-number bounds for conforming P_k and Q_k discretizations with explicit polynomial-degree dependence.
Test on structured triangular/quadrilateral FEM meshes and polygonal VEM meshes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments up to polynomial degree k=9 show scalable behavior, and RGDSW reduces coarse problem dimension by about a factor of three while keeping competitive iteration counts.
infographic.watch_item: The reported robustness is for the 2D Poisson problem, so performance may differ for more complex PDEs, 3D geometries, or strongly heterogeneous coefficients.
infographic.paper_title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D

title: Finite Volume Convergence for a Heat Equation with a Measure-Valued Source
authors: Matthias Gobbert, Martin Kružík, Andreas Meister, Michael Muscedere
abstract: Past work with Tom Seidman analyzed the spatial convergence order of the numerical finite element method applied to time-dependent diffusion-reaction equations with a measure-valued source term. For smooth source terms, the numerical method has second-order accuracy, but the non-smooth source terms introduce a limitation of the order that depends on the spatial dimension. This work in honor of Tom extends the analysis to the finite volume method in its clas- sical two-point flux form and shows that the regularity of the source term reduces the convergence order to 1 in two and 0.5 in three spatial dimensions which is reduced from the nominal second-order and depends on the space dimension. Computational tests with a point source modeled by a Dirac delta distribution exhibit the behavior predicted by the analytical results.

infographic.key_insight: A classical two-point finite volume method loses its nominal second-order accuracy when the heat equation includes a measure-valued source, with convergence limited by spatial dimension.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For simulations with point loads or other singular sources, engineers should expect reduced mesh-convergence rates and choose discretizations accordingly.
method: Analyze finite volume convergence for a time-dependent diffusion-reaction/heat equation with measure-valued forcing
Extend prior finite-element theory to the classical two-point flux finite volume scheme
Compare theoretical convergence limits in 2D and 3D with computational tests using a Dirac delta source
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports computational tests with a Dirac delta point source that match the predicted reduced convergence rates: order 1 in two dimensions and 0.5 in three dimensions.
infographic.watch_item: The main limitation is that singular or measure-valued sources can sharply reduce accuracy, so standard refinement may not recover second-order behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Finite Volume Convergence for a Heat Equation with a Measure-Valued Source

title: Stability analysis of the steady solution for incompressible lid-driven cavity flow
authors: Dmitri Lomasov, Petr Vabishchevich
abstract: Steady solutions at high Reynolds numbers are computed using an iterative method that linearizes the nonlinear convective terms. This linearization reduces the original nonlinear boundary-value problem to a sequence of linear problems, one solved at each iteration, thereby improving the numerical robustness of the algorithm and enabling convergence over a wide range of governing parameters. The stability of steady incompressible fluid flows is studied within the framework of a linear problem for perturbations. The original steady velocity and pressure fields are subjected to small perturbations, after which the equations are linearized with respect to the perturbations. The resulting linear problem allows one to analyze the evolution of small perturbations and to establish whether the steady solutions under consideration are stable with respect to infinitesimal perturbations. In this work, the computational implementation is based on spatial discretization by the finite element method on triangular meshes. The stability of the obtained solutions is analyzed by solving a generalized algebraic eigenvalue problem formed after discretization of the linear problem for perturbations. The presence of eigenvalues with positive real part indicates instability, whereas their absence indicates stability. Calculations were performed on a sequence of refined meshes at various Reynolds numbers for the flow in a square cavity.

infographic.key_insight: The paper computes steady lid-driven cavity flows with a linearized iterative solver and tests their stability by checking eigenvalues of the discretized perturbation problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical way to assess when high-Reynolds-number cavity-flow solutions are physically reliable or unstable in finite-element simulations.
method: Linearize the nonlinear convective terms and solve a sequence of linear steady-state problems.
Apply small perturbations to the steady velocity and pressure fields and linearize the perturbation equations.
Discretize on triangular finite-element meshes and solve the resulting generalized eigenvalue problem.
infographic.evidence_signal: Stability was evaluated on a sequence of refined meshes across multiple Reynolds numbers for square-cavity flow, using the presence of eigenvalues with positive real part as the instability criterion.
infographic.watch_item: Stability conclusions depend on mesh refinement and eigenvalue accuracy, so coarse discretization may miss critical unstable modes.
infographic.paper_title: Stability analysis of the steady solution for incompressible lid-driven cavity flow

title: Galerkin finite element method for time fractional diffusion-wave equations with constant time delay
authors: Xuan Li, Kaile Qiu, Chaobao Huang, Weiping Bu
abstract: This paper studies numerical methods for the time fractional diffusion-wave equations with the constant delay. Using a symmetric fractional-order reduction technique and introducing the auxiliary variable $w$, we reformulate the original problem as an equivalent coupled system and for the first time carry out a rigorous regularity analysis of $w$. Based on the symmetric graded time mesh, the coupled problem is discretised by the $L1$ scheme in time and a standard finite element method in space, and the stability result of the developed fully discrete finite element scheme is established by means of a discrete fractional Grönwall inequality. Furthermore, we derive a new comparison principle and reconstruct a new barrier function on each interval $((k-1)τ,kτ]$, $1\le k\le K$ according to the properties of the symmetric graded mesh. Based on the new barrier function, we obtain new relevant properties, which lead to a novel and crucial stability property for the discrete fractional operator. Combining the obtained local truncation error in time gives a local error estimate for the fully discrete finite element scheme, which shows that our convergence result provides a unified framework that seamlessly encompasses both pointwise-in-time error estimates on uniform meshes and global-in-time error estimates on symmetrical graded meshes. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical results.

infographic.key_insight: A symmetric graded-mesh FEM with L1 time stepping and an auxiliary-variable reformulation yields a stable and convergent solver for time-fractional diffusion-wave equations with constant delay.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical discretization framework for delayed anomalous-diffusion and wave-like processes where standard time stepping can lose accuracy or stability.
method: Reformulate the delayed fractional PDE as an equivalent coupled system using a symmetric fractional-order reduction and auxiliary variable w.
Discretize time with the L1 scheme on a symmetric graded mesh and space with standard finite elements.
Prove stability via a discrete fractional Grönwall inequality and derive local error estimates using a new barrier-function comparison principle.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports theoretical stability and error estimates, and states that numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The method depends on symmetric graded time meshes and a carefully constructed barrier-function analysis, so implementation is more specialized than standard uniform-mesh FEM.
infographic.paper_title: Galerkin finite element method for time fractional diffusion-wave equations with constant time delay
